title: How hands work: grip, sensation and coordination
intro: Hands combine movement, touch and strength for tasks from fastening a button to lifting a bag. Their function depends on bones, joints, tendons, muscles, nerves and circulation working together; pain or numbness cannot be explained by appearance alone.

sections.heading: Bones and joints
paragraphs: The wrist, palm and fingers form linked levers. The thumb can oppose the fingers, enabling precision pinch and broader grips. Joint shape and ligaments guide motion and stability rather than allowing unlimited bending.

sections.heading: Muscles and tendons
paragraphs: Many finger-moving muscles lie in the forearm and pull long tendons. Smaller hand muscles refine movement. Flexor and extensor tendons coordinate bending and straightening, so a small deep cut can impair movement far beyond its visible size.

sections.heading: Nerves and touch
paragraphs: Nerves provide sensation and muscle control. Touch helps judge pressure and avoid injury; numbness may reduce protection even if strength seems adequate. Nerve compression and other disorders require examination, not diagnosis from a single tingling finger.

sections.heading: Skin and circulation
paragraphs: Skin, nails and soft tissue protect vulnerable structures, while vessels supply oxygen. Cold, color change, swelling and wounds need attention. A ring can become dangerously tight after injury; seek help early if it cannot be removed safely.

sections.heading: Supporting function
paragraphs: Adapt painful tasks, use manageable loads and avoid forcing an injured finger. Hand therapy may help selected conditions. New inability to move after a cut, severe deformity, spreading infection or a cold pale numb finger needs urgent assessment. Before a consultation, note when a symptom began, what makes it better or worse, and how it affects ordinary activities. Bring previous reports if available. Ask the professional to connect the explanation to your own findings rather than assuming that a general description establishes a diagnosis.

examples.title: A practical example
examples.text: In this hypothetical example, Mira uses a larger handle to reduce discomfort while arranging assessment for persistent grip pain, rather than forcing through every task.

examples.title: Another practical example
examples.text: In this hypothetical example, Arben has a small palm cut and cannot bend a finger normally. He seeks urgent care because tendon damage can be hidden beneath a small wound.
